claim: When customers search, Amazon says it shows them products it thinks they will be most satisfied with.
evidence: When customers search in our store for something to buy, we show them products we think they’ll be most satisfied with.

claim: Amazon refines search results using customer actions, such as how frequently an item was purchased by other customers.
evidence: based on factors like customer actions (such as how frequently an item was purchased by other customers)

claim: Amazon names the product's price, delivery speed, and what is hot and new as factors.
evidence: the product’s price, delivery speed, what’s hot and new

claim: Amazon names measures of post-purchase satisfaction, such as return rates, as a factor.
evidence: measures of post-purchase satisfaction like return rates

claim: When customers are dissatisfied, Amazon ranks products customers are more likely to love higher in search results.
evidence: we rank other products—ones we’ve determined customers are more likely to love—higher in search results.

claim: Amazon Australia says its search predictions use information about the item, such as the title, price and description.
evidence: information about the item (such as the title, price, and description)

claim: Amazon says its systems now better understand the intent behind a customer's search.
evidence: Our systems now better understand the intent behind a customer's search.

claim: Amazon says the Featured Offer is chosen on criteria such as low price including delivery and fast delivery, and customer preference determines it.
evidence: Customer preference determines which offer we feature.

evidence: Items that customers can find in the search results but are not necessarily on sale.

evidence: generic_keyword: 500 bytes

claim: Item Highlights are fully searchable.

claim: Search Catalog Performance helps identify drop-off points in product discoverability and sales conversion.

claim: Keywords can be used in product titles, descriptions, bullet points and more.
